title: Scenario 1: Adoption

support.label: Worked example
support.description: A senior analyst walks you through the first issue. You find the second one yourself, with hints if you need them.

briefing.from: Dana Reyes, Director of Digital Lending, Harborline Bank
briefing.subject: Is Flex adoption on track?
body: Harborline Flex launched in the mobile app 12 weeks ago. In week 5 we expanded eligibility to a much larger group of debit and credit customers.
The weekly report says the plan creation rate dropped from about 4.5% to under 3%, and a member of the leadership team has asked whether we should pull the feature.
Before Thursday's launch review, I need your read: is adoption on track, and what should we do next?

metrics.name: Plan creation rate among eligible customers shown the offer
metrics.feedback: This is the core adoption rate: plans created divided by the eligible customers who actually saw the offer. It has a clear denominator, so it can be compared over time, as long as the population stays comparable.

metrics.name: New Flex users per week, by product
metrics.feedback: A count, but a useful one when read by product: it shows which of the three products is driving adoption. Pair it with a rate so growth in reach is not mistaken for growth in interest.

metrics.name: Share of eligible customers who have used Flex at least once
metrics.feedback: Penetration: a cumulative adoption measure with a clear denominator. It shows how much of the reachable market has tried the feature.

metrics.name: Median days from first seeing the offer to first plan
metrics.feedback: Time to adopt. Shorter is better, and it is defined relative to a clear starting event, so it is comparable across cohorts.

metrics.name: Offer opt-out rate (customers who hide or decline the offer)
metrics.feedback: A guardrail: if it rises, the offer is reaching people who do not want it. Growth bought with a rising opt-out rate can damage the customer relationship.

metrics.name: Complaints per 1,000 plans created
metrics.feedback: A guardrail normalized by volume. Raw complaint counts rise with any growth; complaints per 1,000 plans tell you whether the experience is getting worse.

metrics.name: Plans cancelled within 14 days
metrics.feedback: A guardrail for regret or confusion at sign-up. A rising early-cancellation share suggests customers did not understand what they agreed to.

metrics.name: Offer impressions
metrics.feedback: Impressions rise whenever the offer is shown to more people, whether or not anyone uses it. On its own it measures reach, not adoption.

metrics.name: Total sign-ups since launch
metrics.feedback: A cumulative count with no denominator. It can only go up, so it cannot tell you whether adoption is improving or slowing.

metrics.name: Views of the Flex information page
metrics.feedback: Page views show curiosity, not adoption. They can rise because of a marketing push without any change in plans created.

metrics.name: Total app sessions
metrics.feedback: App sessions are driven by everything in the app. A change in sessions says almost nothing about Flex specifically.

metrics.name: Push notifications sent about Flex
metrics.feedback: This measures the bank's own activity, not customer behavior. Sending more notifications is an input, not an outcome.

segment_note: Newly eligible customers only exist from week 5, when eligibility was expanded.

charts.title: Plan creation rate (plans ÷ customers shown the offer)
Offer opt-out rate (opt-outs ÷ customers shown the offer)

s1_base: Start with the chart that worried leadership: the plan creation rate drops sharply in week 5.
Before concluding that customers lost interest, check the denominator. Look at 'Customers shown the offer': it more than doubled in the same week. That is the eligibility expansion.

Now use the segment filter and choose 'Originally eligible'. The rate for the original base is steady at about 4.5% and even rising. The blended rate fell because a large new group with a lower rate joined the base.
So the right flag is on the creation-rate chart, weeks 5 to 12, with the issue type 'The base changed (denominator shift)'. Add that flag below to continue.

hints.s1_base: Compare the week the rate dropped with the week the number of customers shown the offer jumped.
hints.s1_optout: Successful growth should not make guardrails worse. Look at the guardrail chart before and after week 5.

decision.question: Based on the dashboard, what do you recommend for Flex?

ship.feedback: Partly right: adoption in the original base is healthy, so there is no case for pulling the feature. But continuing as is ignores the opt-out rate, which more than doubled after the expansion.

iterate.feedback: This matches the expert view. The feature is healthy in its original base; the drop in the blended rate is a denominator effect. The expansion reached customers who convert less and opt out more, so the targeting for that group should change.

rollback.feedback: This is the conclusion the misleading headline invites. The original base still converts at about 4.5% and improving, so pulling the feature would discard a working product because of how the number was calculated.

evidence.text: The creation rate for originally eligible customers stayed around 4.5% and rose slightly.
Newly eligible customers convert at roughly a third of the original rate.
The offer opt-out rate more than doubled after week 5.
Offer impressions more than doubled after week 5.
evidence.why: This shows the reach grew, not that customers want the feature; on its own it is a vanity signal.

evidence.text: Total plans created per week rose after week 5.
evidence.why: True, but it is a count that grows with reach. It does not distinguish a healthier feature from a bigger audience.

evidence.text: Flex 4 is the most popular of the three products.
evidence.why: Accurate, but it does not bear on whether adoption is on track or what to do next.

decision.expert_rationale: Iterate. The drop in the plan creation rate from about 4.5% to under 3% is a denominator effect, not a loss of interest: eligibility expansion in week 5 roughly doubled the customers shown the offer, and the newly eligible group converts at about 1.4%. Among originally eligible customers, the rate held near 4.5% and edged up, so the feature is working for its intended audience and should not be pulled. However, the expansion has a cost: the offer opt-out rate rose from about 0.6% to about 1.5%, driven by the new group. I recommend keeping Flex live, reporting adoption separately for each eligibility cohort going forward, and narrowing or re-targeting the offer for newly eligible customers. If the opt-out rate in the new cohort does not fall below 1% within four weeks of re-targeting, we should restrict eligibility back toward the original base.
